info.bio: Orchestral Manoeuvres In The Dark (OMD) es una banda electrónica inglesa formada en Wirral, Merseyside en 1978. La banda está compuesta por los cofundadores Andy McCluskey (voz, bajo) y Paul Humphreys (teclados, voz), junto con Martin Cooper (varios instrumentos) y Stuart Kershaw (batería). McCluskey y Humphreys se conocieron en la escuela primaria en Meols a principios de la década de 1960, y a mediados de la década de 1970, cuando eran adolescentes

scenes.name: Synthpop británico
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Con The Human League a la cabeza, el auge de 1981-1982: los sintetizadores baratos (el Wasp), las cajas de ritmos Linn y las baterías Simmons democratizan la electrónica, al punto de que el sindicato de músicos propone racionarlos. Instrumento andrógino frente a la guitarra fálica, refugio para los adolescentes que se sentían distintos. Soft Cell lleva la sordidez neoyorquina de Suicide a Leeds («Tainted Love», «Bedsitter», Non-Stop Erotic Cabaret); Japan, máscaras de dandi de Catford, pasa del glam desfasado a la belleza escultural de «Ghosts»; OMD, Pete Shelley («Homosapien»), y Depeche Mode, de chicos inocentes de Basildon en Mute a la política y el sadomasoquismo de «Everything Counts» y «Master and Servant». Hacia 1983 el diluvio de grupos mediocres provoca la reacción y vuelven las guitarras.

scenes.name: Synth-pop y new romantics
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Todo empieza con los instrumentos electrónicos, el futurismo melódico de Eno y los ritmos robóticos de Kraftwerk: el synth-pop es quizá el acontecimiento más importante de la música melódica desde el Mersey-beat. The Buggles («Video Killed The Radio Star»), Gary Numan, Yellow Magic Orchestra, OMD, Depeche Mode, Human League; con Soft Cell llega el diluvio y el dúo de teclista y cantante se impone (Eurythmics, Yazoo, Erasure, Pet Shop Boys). Flying Lizards y New Order («Blue Monday»). Los nuevos ídolos adolescentes, los new romantics: Duran Duran, Culture Club, Thompson Twins, Tears For Fears, ABC, Heaven 17.

mentions.text: …del northern soul, "Tainted Love", luego de lo cual lograron rápidamente otros dos éxitos en Inglaterra con "Bedsitter" y "Say Helio Wave Goodbye". Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, un dúo melódico de Liverpool, aunque cada vez más pretencioso, especializado en la música con sintetizadores, tuvo tres éxitos seguidos en el Top 5…

mentions.author: Piero Scaruffi
mentions.text: …with albums such as Solid State Survivor (1979). Synth-pop was perhaps the single most significant event in melodic music since Mersey-beat. Orchestral Manoeuvres In The Dark (keyboardists Paul Humphreys and Andy McCluskey) were emblematic in the way their synth+vocals equation progressed from the catchy mini-symphonies…

podcast.title: Kraftwerk's Influence (1975)
podcast.body: Andy McCluskey's life was transformed after seeing Kraftwerk perform at the Liverpool Empire on September 11, 1975. This experience inspired the band to pursue alternative electronic music, though Paul Humphreys, being 15, missed the concert due to his mother's age restrictions. "No, we got fascinated by doing alternative music inspired by Kraftwerk and other German rights."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Early Band Name: Hitler's Underpants (Pre-1976)
podcast.body: Before OMD, the band members were in a group with the name "Hitler's Underpants," which they acknowledge as the "worst bad name ever." "This was before. I mean, I'm sorry. I once named that the worst bad name ever. Yeah, and it is. But we can confidently claim that once upon a time we were in Hitler's underpants."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Working-Class Origins & DIY Synths (1976)
podcast.body: Paul Humphreys and Andy McCluskey, from the outskirts of Liverpool, couldn't afford expensive synthesizers. Paul, with a hobby in electronics, would scavenge old radios from relatives to create "noise making machines" that functioned as early, non-keyboard synthesizers, though their sounds were inconsistent. "We were actually playing synths because we couldn't afford one. We were playing all these noise. My hobby was electronics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Unexpected Songwriting Process for "If You Leave" (1986)
podcast.body: The band wrote their biggest North American hit, "If You Leave," in a single day at Larabee Studios under extreme time pressure and without their own instruments. Paul Humphreys composed on a piano, which was a rare occurrence, while Andy McCluskey wrote lyrics, a process likened to "Tin Pan Alley Song Riders." "Paul sat down at a piano, which he never does to riveting. And I sat next to him and started writing words and we, like, we've called Tin Pan Ali Song Riders and gathered around the piano."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Graceful Retirement (1996)
podcast.body: The band had a solid run from 1978 until their dissolution in October 1996. They "gracefully retired" because Britpop was popular, and 80s synthesizer bands were no longer relevant to audiences. "The kids were all about Britpop and a synthesizer band from the 80s just didn't cut it anymore, so the group gracefully retired."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Reunion for Classic Album Tour (2006)
podcast.body: The original lineup reunited on January 1, 2006, after being apart for nine years, three months, and one day. The impetus was serious financial offers to perform their 1981 album "Architecture's and Morality" in its entirety on tour. "The original lineup had received some serious offers to perform their 1981 album, Architecture's and Morality in full on a tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Association with Early Synth Pop
podcast.body: OMD (Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark) is cited as an example of a band representing the first wave of Synth Pop, which is now largely synonymous with the generally accepted definition of New Wave. This association marks a period from the late 1970s to mid-1980s. "Lo que hacía a OEMD, lo que hacía en la expresión Boy y lo que hacía New Order."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Que es el New Wave

podcast.title: CR-78 Usage
podcast.body: OMD (Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark) made use of the Roland CR-78 drum machine in their music, indicative of its influence on techno-pop and electronic genres in the early 1980s. "OMD"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the Drum Machine

podcast.title: Challenges of Early Live Performances (1970s-1980s)
podcast.body: Performing live with early, finicky electronic gear was terrifying for the band, as something would invariably break down. Andy McCluskey resorted to telling jokes to the audience to fill the gaps while the band members frantically tried to fix or reprogram equipment. Monophonic synths required constant, difficult patching between songs using flashlights. "It was terrifying. Actually, it was terrifying and something would always break down. And I ended up having to have a collection of jokes to tell. The audience to fill in the gaps while they were trying to fix something or get something sorted out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Continued Togetherness Post-Reunion
podcast.body: Following their reunion, the band has managed to stay together. "And they've kept it together since then too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: Drummer's Unique Style (Early Albums)
podcast.body: For their first three albums, drummer Paul Malcolm Holmes was instructed not to play a full kit to avoid "rock and roll spillage." Instead, he had to play the bass drum, snare drum, and hi-hat separately to achieve a syncopated, drum-machine-like sound. They even forbade him from using a cymbal as it was considered a "rock and roll cliche." "So Paul Malcolm Holmes used to have to play the bass drum on its own, then the snare drum, then the hi-hat. We wouldn't even let him have a symbol for the first three albums because they were a rock and roll cliche."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Early 80s Alt Rock Example
podcast.body: This band is cited as an example of early 1980s Alt Rock, characterized by its use of synthesizers and a "fancy name," which The Smiths deliberately contrasted with their own plain naming convention and guitar-driven sound. "Because back in the early 80s, Alt Rock was all about synthesizers played by bands with fancy names like orchestral maneuvers in the dark and de Pesh mode."

srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

podcast.title: Early-Mid 80s Hit String
podcast.body: They achieved a string of successful hits throughout the early and middle 1980s. "who had a string of hits through the early and middle 80s."

srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: First Gig at Erics Club (Year Unspecified)
podcast.body: The band played their inaugural gig at Erics, a renowned basement club in Liverpool where many influential bands like The Clash, Sex Pistols, Devo, Pere Ubu, The Cure, and XTC performed. Erics had an open-door policy on Thursday nights, allowing unpaid members to showcase their music. "We used to go to a club in Liverpool called Erics, which was great. A very famous club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: First Musical Instruments (Year Unspecified)
podcast.body: Andy bought a basic guitar with his 16th birthday money. The band's noise-making evolved into more musical compositions when Andy acquired a cheap Selma Pianotron (a reed-based electric piano) for 25 pounds and a Vox Jaguar organ for 35 pounds, both second-hand. "It became musical when I got a cheap electric piano and an organ. Do you remember what that year was? I mean, everybody's fabulous. You know what exactly was it? It was a Selma piano tron, which was like a reed-based piano."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Futurist Philosophy
podcast.body: OMD, along with other similar artists, aimed to look toward a "brave new future," with their music sometimes labeled "futurist," in contrast to a perceived undesirable present. "But for OMD, and others like them, the present sucked. Let's look to a brave new future. In fact, some people call music like this futurist."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 7

podcast.title: Happy, Naive Worldview
podcast.body: Similar to Depeche Mode, the band was characterized by a happy, almost naive worldview, reflecting a more optimistic second wave of electronic music. "And like Depeche Mode, they had a happy, almost naive worldview."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Influence on Trent Reznor
podcast.body: OMD's synthesizers and drum machines were a significant influence on Trent Reznor, contributing to his preference for electronic music over punk and inspiring his path toward becoming a musician. "But the synthesizers and drum machines of the human league and OMD and Depeche mode. Now that was really cool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Deep Dark Secrets of Nine Inch Nails

podcast.title: Intentional Pompous Name
podcast.body: The band intentionally chose what was considered "the most pompous name and history of music" by design. "The band with the most pompous name and history of music, which was completely by design."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 2

podcast.title: John Hughes Movie Soundtrack Success
podcast.body: OMD followed Simple Minds in successfully soundtracking a John Hughes movie, *Pretty in Pink*, with their song "If You Leave." "Or orchestral maneuvers in the dark, better known as OMD, who followed in simple minds footsteps and soundtracked a John Hughes movie, Pretty in Pink."

srcs.episode: The British Are Charting Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Kraftwerk Influence
podcast.body: OMD (Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark) is presented as an example of early 80s techno pop that was influenced by Kraftwerk, illustrating the German band's impact on the nascent electronic pop scene. "Early 80s techno pop like OMD and Soft Cell. Craftwork."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Explaining Krautrock

podcast.title: Live Performance Setup
podcast.body: During live performances, McCluskey and Humphreys surrounded themselves with synthesizers, signal generators, oscilloscopes, and a reel-to-reel tape recorder named Winston, creating an unusual sight even for the open-minded punk era. "And when they played live McCluskey and Humphrey's surround of themselves with not only synthesizers, but signal generators and oscilloscopes and a real-to-real tape recorder named Winston."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 7

podcast.title: Liverpool-Based All-Electronic Group
podcast.body: The band is an all-electronic group originating from Liverpool. "Orcestral maneuvers in the dark, the all-electronic group from Liverpool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Moroder's Influence
podcast.body: OMD (Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark) is noted as one of the many technopop bands that emerged in the years following Giorgio Moroder's pioneering work with synthesizers and his production of "I Feel Love" for Donna Summer. Moroder's innovative electronic sound was a direct inspiration for their musical direction. "You can actually draw a straight line from that song through to Dopech mode and OMD and the human league and dozens and dozens of other technopop bands that would emerge in the next few years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Key Alt-Rock Movie Soundtracks

podcast.title: Museum Collection (Contemporary)
podcast.body: OMD's vintage equipment, including their Korg Micro Preset and Roland CR-78, is being collected for exhibition at the British Music Experience Museum in Liverpool, despite its appearance as "the biggest pile of junk ever." "We still have the Corg Micro preset is now in a museum in Liverpool. In fact, it's all going into, back into another museum in Liverpool because there's the British Music Experience Museum in Liverpool and they're doing an exhibition of us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Newspaper Headline (Year Unspecified)
podcast.body: The band was the subject of a unique newspaper headline in a small town UK paper. When birds (referred to as "castles") built a nest, the headline read: "Four Castles Manoeuvres in the Dark," a play on their band name. "And the headline was, four castles man uvres in the dark."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: North American Success and John Hughes (1980s)
podcast.body: After signing with A&M Records, OMD gained significant traction in North America, particularly Canada. Their profile was further boosted when filmmaker John Hughes began featuring their music in his films, first with "Tesla Girls" in "Weird Science," and then by commissioning a song for "Pretty in Pink." "We moved to A&M and that's when they started to push us. And then two years into our A&M career, yeah, John Hughes came along."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Origin and Name Changes
podcast.body: The band, formed in 1977 by Andy McCluskey and Paul Humphreys, initially went by the name "The Id." After becoming "firmly hooked on the joys of electronics," they renamed themselves "VCLXI," after a transistor part, before adopting their "deliberately pretentious name" in the fall of 1978. "To begin as the id, and were formed by Andy McCluskey and Paul Humphrey's 1977. They started playing in and around Liverpool, especially at a hot club called Erics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 7

podcast.title: Origin of Band Name (Year Unspecified)
podcast.body: The name "Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark" was hastily chosen from a song title idea written on Andy McCluskey's bedroom wall, just before their first gig at Erics. They sought a name that conveyed their "weird" electronic sound, distinct from punk, disco, or pop, and almost chose "Margaret Thatcher's Afterbirth." "So we called ourselves orchestral music in the dark, utterly pretentious. The only thing I'll say is it could have been worse right below it was Margaret Fatches after birth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Pioneering 80s Keyboard-Bass Alt Rock
podcast.body: OMD was identified as one of the "keyboard bass bands" from 25 years prior to the 2000s that alternative audiences danced to, representing the electronic and dance-oriented aspects of 80s alt rock that resurfaced in the oughts. "25 years earlier, long before Grunge guitars took over, alternative kids danced to keyboard bass bands like Depeche Mode, New Order, OMD, Durand Iran, the Human League, Eurasia, Eurythmics, and so many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00s Part 4: Variety Returns

podcast.title: Pioneering All-Electronic New Wave
podcast.body: OMD was identified as one of the most significant bands of the Technopop era and among the first of the new wave generation to fully embrace all-electronic sounds. Their approach was rooted in a punk rock aesthetic, despite limited traditional musical ability, focusing on creating new sounds with synthesizers. "The perfect example of late 70s technopop from orchestral maneuvers in the dark, they were one of the first of the new wave generation to turn to all electronic sounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 2: Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Punk Sensibility in Synthesizer Use
podcast.body: Members Andy McCluskey and Paul Humphreys described their self-taught approach to music-making with synthesizers as having a "punk rock aesthetic." Instead of merely thrashing a guitar, they would play with two fingers on synths, creating sounds the "human brain had never heard before," which they found exciting compared to "rock and roll cliches" of traditional instrumentation. "But you were coming up with... You were coming up with sounds that the human brain had never heard before, which was the cool thing about these new machines. That was the exciting thing about using electronics was it gave us access to a pallet of sounds that were new and exciting, rather than just repeating what we saw in the mid to late 70s, is, you know, just rock and roll cliches."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 2: Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Punk Sensibility of Electronic Music (1970s-1980s)
podcast.body: The band viewed their use of synths, playing with just two fingers, as an electronic equivalent to the punk rock aesthetic of thrashing a single guitar chord. They embraced electronics to create novel sounds, rejecting what they saw as "rock and roll cliches" of guitar, bass, and drums. "It was the punk sensibility, you know, just, instead of just thrashing one chord on a guitar, we were just playing with two fingers on synths and it was the same thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Resistance from Traditionalists (1970s-1980s)
podcast.body: OMD faced significant backlash and criticism from those who argued that synthesizer music wasn't "real music" because machines were doing the work. They were deemed not "authentic, not manly, not rock and roll or sweaty enough." The Musicians Union also opposed them, accusing them of taking jobs from orchestral musicians, leading OMD to ironically display "Keep Music Live" stickers on their tape machine. "Yeah, well, this was it. We were up against this all the time. Synthesizer music is not real music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Signed by Rob Gretton to Factory Records
podcast.body: OMD (Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark) was one of the groups that signed with Factory Records through the influence of Rob Gretton. Gretton was instrumental in bringing various talented acts to the label, bolstering its roster.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock

podcast.title: Studio Ownership
podcast.body: Andy McCluskey, a member of Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark, owned the Pink Museum Studio in Manchester, where Oasis conducted their first studio sessions. "The first sessions were at a Manchester place called Pink Museum Studio, which was owned by Andy McCluskey of orchestral maneuvers in the dark."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: In the Studio with Oasis

podcast.title: Upbeat Electronic Pop
podcast.body: Their first single, released in May 1979, showcased a unique style of electronic pop music that, unlike Kraftwerk's sound, was upbeat, happy, and described as "holds full." "Not only was their music completely electronic, but unlike craftwork, OMD's band of pop music was upbeat, happy, and there we say it. Holds full."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 7

podcast.title: Winston the 4-track (Early Days)
podcast.body: To compensate for their inability to find other musicians to play with them, OMD used a reel-to-reel 4-track tape machine named Winston (after Winston Smith from George Orwell's "1984") as "the rest of the band" during live shows. They borrowed it from Paul Humphreys' friend, Paul Collister, who had a home studio. "We needed a tape machine to be the rest of the band to put the drums on and anything we couldn't play as two of us. So we used to borrow, I think Paul borrowed one of his aunts, real to real to some end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

podcast.title: Winston the Tape Machine
podcast.body: Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark affectionately named their reel-to-reel tape machine "Winston." This machine was used on stage to play back pre-recorded rhythm tracks, a common practice for bands during the techno pop era. "Orcastrol maneuvers in the dark called their tape machine Winston."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 10

xref.title: Band Name Origin
xref.body: The name "The Smiths" was deliberately chosen because Morrissey and Marr couldn't think of anything more plain or boring, making a statement against the fancy names of other Alt Rock bands of the early 80s like Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark and Depeche Mode. It was also a homage to New York poet Patti Smith, one of Morrissey's heroes, and possibly a nod to a 1960s Manchester nightclub called Mr. Smiths. "They chose the name the Smiths because they couldn't think of anything more plain or anything more boring. That was very deliberate."
